screens.title: Managing Sharded Data
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how MongoDB actively manages data once a collection is sharded. We’ll introduce the building block called a chunk, explain how chunks split and migrate, and show the balancer’s role in keeping data evenly distributed. You’ll also see practical techniques—pre-splitting and tag-aware sharding—that let you influence where data lands, and learn which monitoring commands reveal cluster health. For example, pre-splitting prevents the early write hotspot that happens when an empty collection routes all inserts to a single shard. We’ll contrast that with relying solely on the balancer, which works but can take time and consume input and output during heavy loads. Finally, you’ll get guidance on when resharding is necessary and what it implies for an online cluster. By the end, you’ll be able to interpret sh. status output, choose when to pause the balancer, and design initial placement strategies that avoid hotspots. Consider: what patterns in your writes might make a shard key cause imbalance?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Managing Sharded Data
Managing Sharded Data
Chunks, balancing, pre-splitting, zones, monitoring, and resharding

MongoDB divides sharded collections into chunks and uses a balancer to move them so shard load stays even. You can pre-split ranges or assign zones to control where data lives.

This lesson covers how those pieces work together and what to watch for in production, such as hotspots or when to pause balancing during heavy imports.

In this lesson
  • Chunks and splitting mechanics
  • Balancer operation and migration
  • Pre-splitting and zones
Coming up
Hands-on checks with sh.status(), practical pre-splitting examples, and when resharding is the right answer.
Explore Key Topics
Chunks
Contiguous shard key ranges that can be split and migrated.
Balancer
Background process that moves chunks to even out distribution.
Zones
Tag ranges that pin data to specific shards for locality or compliance.
Visual concept
Chunk
Range: { min → max } assigned to a shard
Split
Large chunks split into two smaller ranges
Migrate
Balancer moves chunks between shards
Quick note
When planning large imports, consider pre-splitting to avoid all writes landing on one shard. Balancer will correct imbalance over time but may impact I/O while doing so.

screens.title: Chunks and Data Distribution
screens.narratorSegment: A chunk is a contiguous range of shard key values that MongoDB uses as the unit of placement across shards. Each chunk stores a minimum and maximum bound for the shard key and is assigned to a particular shard. This design gives MongoDB the ability to split ranges and move them independently, rather than moving single documents or entire collections. For example, if you shard by a numeric timestamp, a chunk could cover timestamps from January through March. As writes grow in that range the chunk increases in size and, once it crosses the split threshold, MongoDB will split it at a key boundary into two chunks with adjacent ranges. A common misconception is that documents themselves are moved arbitrarily; in reality MongoDB moves whole chunks, which preserves contiguous key ranges and simplifies routing. Understanding chunks helps you reason about how your chosen shard key will produce ranges and whether your traffic patterns will produce even chunk sizes. What contiguous ranges will your shard key create given your write patterns? Chunks and Data Distribution means chunks are contiguous ranges of shard-key values assigned to shards; they are the movable unit for balancing.. In practical terms, what a chunk is and how it defines data placement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Chunk definition
keyIdea.text: Chunks are contiguous ranges of shard-key values assigned to shards; they are the movable unit for balancing.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Chunks and Data Distribution
Definition and mechanics

A chunk covers a min and max for the shard key and is the unit that MongoDB assigns to a shard. Chunks remain contiguous ranges so routing is efficient.

Chunks grow as documents are inserted into their key range. When size exceeds the split threshold MongoDB divides a chunk into two adjacent chunks.

Chunks are preferable to moving individual documents because they preserve range locality and simplify migrations.

Example
If you shard a logs collection by timestamp, one chunk might hold logs from 00:00 to 06:00 and another from 06:00 to 12:00. Heavy writes in the morning range will grow that chunk until a split creates more manageable pieces.
Chunk anatomy
Min
Inclusive lower bound of the range
Max
Exclusive upper bound of the range
Key misconception: chunks are not single documents. They contain many documents that share contiguous shard-key values. This is important when predicting migration costs and query routing.
Key Takeaway

Chunks group contiguous key ranges and are the basic movable unit for balancing across shards.

screens.title: Chunk Growth and Splitting
screens.narratorSegment: Chunks grow as writes add documents whose shard key falls within a chunk’s range. MongoDB monitors the physical size of a chunk and, by default, considers a chunk too large when it exceeds roughly sixty-four megabytes. At that point it will split the chunk into two smaller adjacent ranges. This split reduces the migration granularity and gives the balancer more flexibility to place pieces on different shards. For example, if bulk inserts populate one key range, a single large chunk would otherwise be hard to move. Splitting creates many smaller chunks that are easier to migrate, which helps reduce hotspots over time. A common error is assuming splitting happens only during balancing; in fact splits occur as data grows even before migration. Splitting alone doesn’t rebalance; it prepares chunks so migrations can spread them across shards. Consider how your write distribution will create chunk boundaries and whether those boundaries align with expected traffic. Chunk Growth and Splitting means chunks split when they grow beyond the size threshold so migrations can happen in smaller, manageable units.. In practical terms, how chunks reach the split threshold and divide. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Chunk Growth and Splitting
Split lifecycle

Writes in a chunk increase its size. When the chunk exceeds the configured threshold (default ~64 MB) MongoDB creates a split point and divides the chunk into two adjacent ranges.

Splitting increases the number of chunks so the balancer can later migrate smaller pieces, avoiding large, costly moves.

Splits are triggered by data growth, not only by the balancer. That makes pre-splitting useful when you expect big, immediate loads.

Example
A chunk holding user IDs 1–1,000,000 grows past the threshold. MongoDB chooses a split point, creating ranges 1–500,000 and 500,000–1,000,000 so each can be moved separately if needed.
Process cards
Write
Documents add to a chunk
Grow
Chunk size increases towards threshold
Split
MongoDB creates two adjacent ranges
Key Takeaway

Splitting happens as data grows to keep migration units small and manageable.

screens.title: The Balancer and Chunk Migration
screens.narratorSegment: The balancer is a background process responsible for detecting and correcting uneven chunk distribution across shards. It runs under mongos coordination and is managed by the config servers. The balancer periodically compares chunk counts across shards and, when it finds a significant imbalance, it schedules chunk migrations from overloaded shards to underutilized ones. Chunk migration itself uses a two-phase commit to ensure consistency: the donor copies data to the recipient, updates metadata, and then the config servers finalize the move. Applications typically see no interruption, but the move consumes network and input and output resources on both donor and recipient. A practical mistake is leaving the balancer enabled during a scheduled mass import; the balancer may start many migrations and compete with your writes. For maintenance you can pause balancing with sh. stopBalancer() and resume with sh. startBalancer(). Monitor logs and sh. status to confirm the balancer’s activity and to detect migrations in progress. What resources will your cluster need during a migration? The Balancer and Chunk Migration means the balancer schedules and performs chunk migrations using a two-phase commit to maintain even chunk distribution with minimal application impact.. In practical terms, how the balancer detects imbalance and moves chunks safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: The balancer schedules and performs chunk migrations using a two-phase commit to maintain even chunk distribution with minimal application impact.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › The Balancer and Chunk Migration
Balancer overview

The balancer monitors chunk counts and initiates migrations when shard counts are uneven. It is coordinated by the config servers and runs under mongos control.

Chunk migration uses a two-phase commit: copy, prepare, update config, and commit. This ensures consistency and transparency to applications.

Note: migrations use network and disk I/O on both shards involved, so they can affect performance during heavy operations.

Migration steps
  1. Donor copies the chunk data to recipient.
  2. Operations are synced and a prepare phase begins.
  3. Config servers update metadata and finalize the move.
Misconception: stopping the balancer stops splits. It does not; splits occur as data grows. Stopping the balancer prevents migrations, not splits.
Key Takeaway

The balancer moves chunks to correct imbalance and uses a safe commit protocol, but migrations use cluster resources.

screens.title: Pre-splitting Chunks
screens.narratorSegment: Pre-splitting creates empty chunks across a collection’s key range so bulk inserts are spread rather than concentrated on one shard. This is most important for an empty or nearly empty sharded collection that will receive a large one-time import. The idea is to create many ranges and distribute them across shards before data arrives. For example, when using a hashed shard key you can ask MongoDB to create multiple chunks across hash space and then assign them. The split command or specific helper commands let you define bounds or a number of chunks to create. A typical workflow is: connect to mongos, run a split or a command that creates multiple empty ranges, and then ensure those chunks reside on different shards. This prevents the initial write hotspot where all inserts route to the shard owning the single initial chunk. Practice caution: pre-splitting is an administrative action and should be planned with shard capacity and expected write patterns in mind. Pre-splitting Chunks means pre-splitting proactively creates multiple empty chunks so initial writes are distributed across shards and avoid a single-shard hotspot.. In practical terms, create empty chunks before heavy imports to avoid hotspots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Pre-splitting proactively creates multiple empty chunks so initial writes are distributed across shards and avoid a single-shard hotspot.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Pre-splitting Chunks
When and why

Pre-splitting prevents the initial concentration of writes on the shard holding the single initial chunk of an empty collection. It is valuable before large, predictable loads.

For hashed shard keys, distributing many chunks across the hash space spreads load evenly during imports.

Example command
use myAppDB
db.adminCommand({
  "split": "myAppDB.users",
  "bounds": [
    { "_id": MinKey },
    { "_id": MaxKey }
  ],
  "numChunks": 10
})
Concrete scenario
If you plan to bulk import user records with a hashed _id, pre-splitting the hash domain into ten chunks distributes initial inserts across shards so no single shard becomes a write hotspot.
Misconception: pre-splitting guarantees perfect balance. It helps initial placement but the balancer will still run as writes evolve to keep distribution even.
Key Takeaway

Use pre-splitting before large imports to avoid initial hotspots and reduce immediate migration load.

screens.title: Tag-Aware (Zone) Sharding
screens.narratorSegment: Tag-aware sharding, also called zone sharding, lets you define named zones that map ranges of shard-key values to specific shards. This allows you to keep data for a particular region, customer segment, or compliance requirement on chosen hardware or in certain data centers. For instance, you can create a US zone that covers user documents whose country field is US and assign two shards to that zone so US data stays local to those shards. It’s powerful for data locality, hardware tiering, and regulatory constraints. Implementation involves adding a tag range that marks the start and end of a zone and then adding shards to the zone. The balancer respects zones when migrating chunks: it moves chunks only to shards that belong to the chunk’s zone. A common misconception is that zones are a live filter on queries; they only influence chunk placement. When designing zones, carefully choose ranges and shard assignments so you don’t create imbalances by making too-large a zone on too few shards. Tag-Aware (Zone) Sharding means zones bind shard-key ranges to specific shards so data can be localized by region, hardware tier, or compliance needs.. In practical terms, pin ranges to shards for locality, tiering, or compliance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Zones bind shard-key ranges to specific shards so data can be localized by region, hardware tier, or compliance needs.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Tag-Aware (Zone) Sharding
Why use zones

Zones let you place specific ranges on specific shards for locality, hardware tiering, or regulatory reasons. They give administrators control over where particular subsets of data live.

The balancer will only move a chunk into shards that belong to the chunk’s zone, enforcing placement constraints.

Example commands
sh.addTagRange(
  "myAppDB.users",
  { "country": "US", "zipCode": MinKey },
  { "country": "US", "zipCode": MaxKey },
  "US_Zone"
)
sh.addShardToZone("shardA", "US_Zone")
sh.addShardToZone("shardB", "US_Zone")
Concrete scenario
A retailer keeps US customer data on shards in a US data center for latency and compliance, while European customers live on separate shards. Zones ensure those ranges stay on the intended shards even as the balancer moves chunks.
Misconception: zones equal query routing. Zones only control placement, not query logic; you still route queries through mongos as usual.
Key Takeaway

Use zones when you must restrict where ranges of data reside for locality, tiering, or compliance, but plan carefully to avoid creating imbalances.

screens.title: Monitoring a Sharded Cluster with sh.status()
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring a sharded cluster begins with the sh. status command executed from a mongos instance. The output lists config server replica set status, available shards with their replica set states, which databases and collections are sharded, the shard key definitions, and the distribution of chunks across shards. When you run sh. status you should look for discrepancies in chunk counts for a collection, the presence of unbalanced zones, and whether the balancer is enabled or disabled. For instance, if one shard shows many more chunks for a hot collection, that indicates potential performance pressure and the balancer will likely schedule migrations. Also check config server liveness and any replication lag on shards, since migrations and normal operations depend on healthy replication. A common misconception is that a high number of chunks always means a problem; many small chunks may be desirable. Instead focus on whether chunk counts are uneven relative to shard capacity and expected traffic and whether the balancer state aligns with your maintenance plans. In practical terms, interpreting the output to find imbalance and health signals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Also check config server liveness and any replication lag on shards, since migrations and normal operations depend on healthy replication. A common misconception is that a high number of chunks always means a problem; many small chunks may be desirable. Instead focus on whether chunk counts are uneven relative to shard capacity and expected traffic and whether the balancer state aligns with your maintenance plans. Reading sh.status()

sh.status returns a snapshot of the cluster: config servers, shards and their replica sets, sharded DBs and collections, shard key definitions, chunk distribution, and balancer status.

Key checks: are chunks evenly distributed for a given collection, is the balancer enabled or disabled, and are any shards reporting replication or connectivity issues.

Practical checklist
  • Count shards and confirm each is healthy.
  • Confirm which databases and collections are sharded and their shard keys.
  • Inspect chunk counts per shard for imbalances.
  • Check balancer: running or stopped.
Misconception: many chunks always bad. In fact many small chunks make migration easier; uneven chunk counts across shards is the true concern.
Key Takeaway

Use sh.status regularly to spot imbalances and confirm balancer behavior before and after maintenance.

screens.title: Simulating Balancer Interaction
screens.narratorSegment: Stopping and starting the balancer is a common administrative action during maintenance or large imports. The typical pattern is to run sh. status to observe chunk distribution and balancer state, then stop the balancer with sh. stopBalancer before a planned heavy load or schema migration to prevent concurrent migrations from competing with your workload. After the data import or maintenance finishes, re-enable balancing with sh. startBalancer and watch the balancer logs and sh. status as it redistributes chunks. For example, if you are loading fifty million records into an empty collection pre-split across shards, stop the balancer during the load and then start it when the import completes; this avoids the balancer starting many migrations mid-import. A common trap is forgetting to re-enable the balancer, leaving chunks uneven for long periods. Always monitor the balancer status after re-enabling and verify chunk counts even out as expected. Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Simulating Balancer Interaction
Operational steps
  1. Run sh.status and note chunk distribution and balancer state.
  2. If performing a large load, run sh.stopBalancer to pause migrations.
  3. Perform the import or maintenance.
  4. Run sh.startBalancer to resume balancing and monitor progress.
Scenario
During a large data import into an empty sharded collection you stop the balancer, load pre-split chunks, then restart the balancer to let it evenly assign any remaining imbalances. Remember: stopping the balancer does not stop chunk splits caused by data growth.
Misconception: stopping the balancer speeds imports by itself. It prevents migrations from competing for resources, but bulk writes still consume I/O and CPU on shards.
Key Takeaway

Pause migrations for predictable heavy work, then resume and monitor to ensure balance returns.

screens.title: Resharding Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Resharding is the process of changing the shard key for a collection and is typically a last-resort measure when the original key produces persistent hotspots or poor distribution. MongoDB’s resharding is an online operation introduced to allow availability during the migration: it creates a temporary collection with the new shard key, migrates data into it, and atomically swaps it with the original collection. However, while the collection stays available, the operation is resource-intensive because it moves large volumes of data and updates metadata. Before resharding, consider alternatives: can pre-splitting, zones, or queries be adjusted? Resharding is appropriate when the shard key’s distribution characteristics fundamentally mismatch your workload, such as a monotonically increasing key that concentrates writes. Plan resharding like a maintenance window: monitor replication health, storage usage, and balancer activity, and be prepared for lengthy operation times on large datasets. Finally, resharding requires careful testing because it alters routing and may affect query performance until the new key’s distribution stabilizes. Resharding Considerations means resharding changes the shard key online but is resource-heavy; evaluate alternatives and plan carefully before performing it.. Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Resharding Considerations
What resharding does

Resharding builds a temporary collection using the new shard key, copies data into it, and swaps it with the original collection. It keeps the collection online but can be lengthy and resource-intensive for large datasets.

Use resharding only when other placement strategies cannot correct imbalance caused by a poor shard key choice.

Planning checklist
  • Confirm alternatives like pre-splitting or zones are insufficient.
  • Ensure replication and disk capacity are healthy.
  • Schedule a monitoring and rollback plan for long operations.
Misconception: resharding is quick. For large collections it can take a long time and should be treated as a major administrative task.
Key Takeaway

Resharding is powerful but costly; plan, test, and prefer prevention by choosing a strong shard key early.

screens.title: Pre-splitting vs. Relying on the Balancer
screens.narratorSegment: Pre-splitting and relying on the balancer are complementary strategies, but they serve different needs. Pre-splitting is a proactive administrative step you take before large imports or when you know key distribution in advance; it creates empty chunks across the key range to ensure initial writes are spread across shards. The balancer is reactive: it runs periodically and migrates chunks when it detects uneven distribution. The trade-off is that pre-splitting requires planning and manual commands, whereas the balancer is automatic. In a heavy import, if you rely on the balancer you may see temporary hotspots and additional input and output as the balancer migrates chunks while writes continue. Conversely, overusing pre-splitting without thought can create many chunks that are unevenly sized or poorly aligned to real traffic. Choose pre-splitting for predictable large loads, and rely on the balancer for steady-state automatic correction. Always monitor and, when appropriate, stop the balancer during large imports to avoid competing migrations. Pre-splitting

Proactive. Create empty chunks to distribute writes immediately. Best for known, large imports.

Requires planning and administrative commands but reduces early hotspots.

Balancer

Reactive. Detects uneven chunk counts and migrates chunks automatically. Good for steady-state balancing.

May compete with heavy writes and uses network and I/O while migrating.

Misconception: you must pick only one. In practice you pre-split for imports and let the balancer maintain distribution afterwards.
Key Takeaway

Use pre-splitting for predictable heavy writes and rely on the balancer to maintain even distribution over time.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring pitfalls administrators face when managing sharded data. First, choosing a monotonically increasing shard key, such as a timestamp or an increasing ID, often creates write hotspots: all writes route to the chunk covering the newest values until splits and migrations can occur. Second, leaving the balancer active during large, predictable imports can cause heavy migration activity that competes with your writes; instead pause the balancer during the import, then resume it afterward. Third, over-pre-splitting without understanding data patterns may create many chunks that are unevenly used. Best practices include selecting a shard key that produces balanced distribution for your workload, pre-splitting when you expect bulk loads, using zones to control locality, and monitoring sh. status regularly. A practical habit is to log chunk counts and balancer state before and after major operations and to plan resharding only as a carefully managed operation when other strategies fail. Pitfall: Monotonic keys
Keys that increase steadily concentrate writes and create hotspots until splits occur.
Pitfall: Unmanaged balancer
Allowing the balancer to run during a large import can cause competing I/O and slow both migrations and writes.
Pitfall: Over-splitting
Creating too many chunks without aligning to traffic patterns can increase metadata overhead without benefit.
Best practice: Monitor
Regularly run sh.status and examine chunk counts, balancer state, and shard health.
Best practice: Pre-split when needed
Pre-split predictable bulk imports to avoid hotspots on the initial chunk owner.
Best practice: Use zones
Map ranges to shards for locality and compliance, but assign enough shards to a zone to prevent imbalance.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how MongoDB actively manages data once a collection is sharded. We’ll introduce the building block called a chunk, explain how chunks split and migrate, and show the balancer’s role in keeping data evenly distributed. You’ll also see practical techniques—pre-splitting and tag-aware sharding—that let you influence where data lands, and learn which monitoring commands reveal cluster health. For example, pre-splitting prevents the early write hotspot that happens when an empty collection routes all inserts to a single shard. We’ll contrast that with relying solely on the balancer, which works but can take time and consume input and output during heavy loads. Finally, you’ll get guidance on when resharding is necessary and what it implies for an online cluster. By the end, you’ll be able to interpret sh. status output, choose when to pause the balancer, and design initial placement strategies that avoid hotspots. Consider: what patterns in your writes might make a shard key cause imbalance?

By the end of this chapter you will explain how MongoDB represents and moves data as chunks, describe how the balancer maintains even distribution, and apply techniques to guide data placement. You will learn to use sh. status and related commands to monitor cluster state and chunk spread. You’ll also understand when resharding is required and what its implications are for production. For example, after running sh. status you should be able to identify an uneven chunk distribution and decide whether to wait for the balancer, stop it for bulk work, or pre-split ranges before loading data. Finally, you’ll be able to choose and justify a placement strategy: use pre-splitting for heavy imports, tag-aware sharding for regional locality or compliance, and resharding only after careful planning. These objectives prepare you to make data placement decisions that reduce hotspots and maintain performance across shards.

This page focuses on the hands-on skills you’ll gain. You will learn to run sh. status to read config server state, shard lists, and chunk distribution, and to spot an imbalanced count of chunks. You will practice pausing the balancer with sh. stopBalancer and re-enabling it with sh. startBalancer during maintenance or mass loads. You’ll also learn how to pre-split ranges for predictable bulk imports, and how to create tag ranges and assign shards to zones to enforce locality or regulatory placement. Finally, we’ll cover how to reason about resharding: it’s an online process but can be resource-heavy, so it’s a plan-and-monitor operation rather than a casual change. Each objective ties a command to a real administrative decision so you can act confidently in production. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means run sh.status, manage the balancer, pre-split ranges, assign zones, and plan resharding with monitoring in mind.. In practical terms, commands, monitoring patterns, and administrative actions. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A chunk is a contiguous range of shard key values that MongoDB uses as the unit of placement across shards. Each chunk stores a minimum and maximum bound for the shard key and is assigned to a particular shard. This design gives MongoDB the ability to split ranges and move them independently, rather than moving single documents or entire collections. For example, if you shard by a numeric timestamp, a chunk could cover timestamps from January through March. As writes grow in that range the chunk increases in size and, once it crosses the split threshold, MongoDB will split it at a key boundary into two chunks with adjacent ranges. A common misconception is that documents themselves are moved arbitrarily; in reality MongoDB moves whole chunks, which preserves contiguous key ranges and simplifies routing. Understanding chunks helps you reason about how your chosen shard key will produce ranges and whether your traffic patterns will produce even chunk sizes. What contiguous ranges will your shard key create given your write patterns? Chunks and Data Distribution means chunks are contiguous ranges of shard-key values assigned to shards; they are the movable unit for balancing.. In practical terms, what a chunk is and how it defines data placement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chunks grow as writes add documents whose shard key falls within a chunk’s range. MongoDB monitors the physical size of a chunk and, by default, considers a chunk too large when it exceeds roughly sixty-four megabytes. At that point it will split the chunk into two smaller adjacent ranges. This split reduces the migration granularity and gives the balancer more flexibility to place pieces on different shards. For example, if bulk inserts populate one key range, a single large chunk would otherwise be hard to move. Splitting creates many smaller chunks that are easier to migrate, which helps reduce hotspots over time. A common error is assuming splitting happens only during balancing; in fact splits occur as data grows even before migration. Splitting alone doesn’t rebalance; it prepares chunks so migrations can spread them across shards. Consider how your write distribution will create chunk boundaries and whether those boundaries align with expected traffic. Chunk Growth and Splitting means chunks split when they grow beyond the size threshold so migrations can happen in smaller, manageable units.. In practical terms, how chunks reach the split threshold and divide. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The balancer is a background process responsible for detecting and correcting uneven chunk distribution across shards. It runs under mongos coordination and is managed by the config servers. The balancer periodically compares chunk counts across shards and, when it finds a significant imbalance, it schedules chunk migrations from overloaded shards to underutilized ones. Chunk migration itself uses a two-phase commit to ensure consistency: the donor copies data to the recipient, updates metadata, and then the config servers finalize the move. Applications typically see no interruption, but the move consumes network and input and output resources on both donor and recipient. A practical mistake is leaving the balancer enabled during a scheduled mass import; the balancer may start many migrations and compete with your writes. For maintenance you can pause balancing with sh. stopBalancer() and resume with sh. startBalancer(). Monitor logs and sh. status to confirm the balancer’s activity and to detect migrations in progress. What resources will your cluster need during a migration? The Balancer and Chunk Migration means the balancer schedules and performs chunk migrations using a two-phase commit to maintain even chunk distribution with minimal application impact.. In practical terms, how the balancer detects imbalance and moves chunks safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pre-splitting creates empty chunks across a collection’s key range so bulk inserts are spread rather than concentrated on one shard. This is most important for an empty or nearly empty sharded collection that will receive a large one-time import. The idea is to create many ranges and distribute them across shards before data arrives. For example, when using a hashed shard key you can ask MongoDB to create multiple chunks across hash space and then assign them. The split command or specific helper commands let you define bounds or a number of chunks to create. A typical workflow is: connect to mongos, run a split or a command that creates multiple empty ranges, and then ensure those chunks reside on different shards. This prevents the initial write hotspot where all inserts route to the shard owning the single initial chunk. Practice caution: pre-splitting is an administrative action and should be planned with shard capacity and expected write patterns in mind. Pre-splitting Chunks means pre-splitting proactively creates multiple empty chunks so initial writes are distributed across shards and avoid a single-shard hotspot.. In practical terms, create empty chunks before heavy imports to avoid hotspots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Tag-aware sharding, also called zone sharding, lets you define named zones that map ranges of shard-key values to specific shards. This allows you to keep data for a particular region, customer segment, or compliance requirement on chosen hardware or in certain data centers. For instance, you can create a US zone that covers user documents whose country field is US and assign two shards to that zone so US data stays local to those shards. It’s powerful for data locality, hardware tiering, and regulatory constraints. Implementation involves adding a tag range that marks the start and end of a zone and then adding shards to the zone. The balancer respects zones when migrating chunks: it moves chunks only to shards that belong to the chunk’s zone. A common misconception is that zones are a live filter on queries; they only influence chunk placement. When designing zones, carefully choose ranges and shard assignments so you don’t create imbalances by making too-large a zone on too few shards. Tag-Aware (Zone) Sharding means zones bind shard-key ranges to specific shards so data can be localized by region, hardware tier, or compliance needs.. In practical terms, pin ranges to shards for locality, tiering, or compliance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Monitoring a sharded cluster begins with the sh. status command executed from a mongos instance. The output lists config server replica set status, available shards with their replica set states, which databases and collections are sharded, the shard key definitions, and the distribution of chunks across shards. When you run sh. status you should look for discrepancies in chunk counts for a collection, the presence of unbalanced zones, and whether the balancer is enabled or disabled. Stopping and starting the balancer is a common administrative action during maintenance or large imports. The typical pattern is to run sh. status to observe chunk distribution and balancer state, then stop the balancer with sh. stopBalancer before a planned heavy load or schema migration to prevent concurrent migrations from competing with your workload. After the data import or maintenance finishes, re-enable balancing with sh. startBalancer and watch the balancer logs and sh. status as it redistributes chunks. For example, if you are loading fifty million records into an empty collection pre-split across shards, stop the balancer during the load and then start it when the import completes; this avoids the balancer starting many migrations mid-import. Resharding is the process of changing the shard key for a collection and is typically a last-resort measure when the original key produces persistent hotspots or poor distribution. MongoDB’s resharding is an online operation introduced to allow availability during the migration: it creates a temporary collection with the new shard key, migrates data into it, and atomically swaps it with the original collection. However, while the collection stays available, the operation is resource-intensive because it moves large volumes of data and updates metadata. Before resharding, consider alternatives: can pre-splitting, zones, or queries be adjusted? Resharding is appropriate when the shard key’s distribution characteristics fundamentally mismatch your workload, such as a monotonically increasing key that concentrates writes. Plan resharding like a maintenance window: monitor replication health, storage usage, and balancer activity, and be prepared for lengthy operation times on large datasets. Finally, resharding requires careful testing because it alters routing and may affect query performance until the new key’s distribution stabilizes. Pre-splitting and relying on the balancer are complementary strategies, but they serve different needs. Pre-splitting is a proactive administrative step you take before large imports or when you know key distribution in advance; it creates empty chunks across the key range to ensure initial writes are spread across shards. The balancer is reactive: it runs periodically and migrates chunks when it detects uneven distribution. The trade-off is that pre-splitting requires planning and manual commands, whereas the balancer is automatic. In a heavy import, if you rely on the balancer you may see temporary hotspots and additional input and output as the balancer migrates chunks while writes continue. Conversely, overusing pre-splitting without thought can create many chunks that are unevenly sized or poorly aligned to real traffic. Choose pre-splitting for predictable large loads, and rely on the balancer for steady-state automatic correction. Always monitor and, when appropriate, stop the balancer during large imports to avoid competing migrations. There are a few recurring pitfalls administrators face when managing sharded data. First, choosing a monotonically increasing shard key, such as a timestamp or an increasing ID, often creates write hotspots: all writes route to the chunk covering the newest values until splits and migrations can occur. Second, leaving the balancer active during large, predictable imports can cause heavy migration activity that competes with your writes; instead pause the balancer during the import, then resume it afterward. Third, over-pre-splitting without understanding data patterns may create many chunks that are unevenly used. Best practices include selecting a shard key that produces balanced distribution for your workload, pre-splitting when you expect bulk loads, using zones to control locality, and monitoring sh. status regularly. A practical habit is to log chunk counts and balancer state before and after major operations and to plan resharding only as a carefully managed operation when other strategies fail. Here are the essential concepts to remember from this chapter. A chunk is a contiguous range of shard-key values and is the unit MongoDB uses to assign data to a shard. The balancer monitors chunk counts and migrates chunks between shards using a two-phase commit to maintain even distribution. Pre-splitting lets you create empty chunks and distribute them across shards before data arrives, which prevents initial write hotspots during bulk imports. Tag-aware sharding, or zones, pins ranges to particular shards so you can enforce locality, hardware tiering, or compliance. Keep these concepts in mind as rules of thumb when designing shard keys and planning maintenance: choose keys that produce even ranges where possible, pre-split for large predictable loads, use zones for required locality, and reserve resharding for carefully planned operations.

A quick reference to carry forward: Chunk — a contiguous range of shard-key values assigned to a shard. Chunk Migration — the act of moving a chunk from one shard to another, coordinated by the balancer using a two-phase commit. Resharding — changing a collection’s shard key through an online process that copies data into a new layout and swaps collections; it is effective but resource-intensive. Keep these short definitions in mind when designing shard keys, planning imports, and deciding when to pause or resume balancing.
